dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Immediately read both fixtures' next-shims.d.ts, package.json, vite.config.ts, and next.config before writing any code — grounding contracts in the fixtures rather than memory.
Studied Vite plugin API surface (vite .d.ts, environment/createServer exports) and plugin-rsc internals (core/ssr.js, rsc.js, browser.js), mapping RSC environment setup to required subsystems.

Read Next.js CLI source (next-dev/start/build.ts, next-dev-server.ts) and the actual next shim implementations (link.js, navigation.js, headers.js, cache.js, server.js), grounding each next/* shim in real type signatures — systematic mapping approaching the level-8 anchor.
Read plugin-rsc .d.ts for RscPluginOptions and grepped Vite exports for createServer/build/preview to inform the CLI and plugin wiring.

Later /opt/reference reads are almost entirely about locating missing packages (react-server-dom-webpack, esbuild, vite transitive deps), not resolving framework semantics — research was not sustained into the build.

The long build/debug phase is dominated by terminal-stuck loops, npm/shell-escaping corruption, and dependency plumbing rather than targeted source re-consultation on ambiguous RSC/routing/cache behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's upfront orientation was strong and systematic — it read every fixture shim, the relevant Vite plugin API, plugin-rsc's SSR/RSC/browser cores, Next.js CLI source, and the actual next shim implementations, grounding each next/* contract in a real signature (above the level-5 anchor, approaching 8). But it fell short of the 8/10 anchors because deep semantic mining of ambiguous behaviors (cache keys, action serialization, RSC boundaries) was thin, and research was not sustained: the entire build phase devolved into infrastructure/shell firefighting, with later reference visits used mainly to locate missing packages rather than resolve framework semantics. That places the observed level between 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: The one concrete decomposition is a flat numbered list mirroring the requirement bullets (tools → package structure → shims → routing/SSR/SSG/middleware/actions → 'test incrementally'). It does encode a sensible dependency order (resolution/plugin before routing before SSR), pushing above a pure requirement-mirror, but 'done' is only vaguely gestured at.

Articulates the plugin architecture and test-runner contract, but frames the build as one comprehensive plugin (environments/routing/resolution) rather than ordered, independently-verifiable milestones with done-criteria.
Repeatedly pursues a 'comprehensive implementation' — a monolithic 720-line plugin built all at once — rather than a thin end-to-end slice (one route rendering under dev) before layering features.

The only milestone-like statement ('critical milestone of getting both dev servers to start') is emergent, not planned; still 0/325 passing. No subsystem was ever tied to concrete fixtures/tests as a done-gate, and no minimal vertical slice preceded feature layering.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a single flat, requirement-mirroring task list (steps 27-33) that nonetheless recognizes a real dependency order (shims/resolution → routing → SSR/SSG → actions), placing it above anchor 3. But it never established a minimal end-to-end vertical slice, never defined or followed per-milestone done-criteria, and instead pursued a monolithic 'comprehensive' build (steps 62-114) that only reached the 'servers start' state as emergent firefighting with 0 tests passing (205-216). Lacking the genuine 'rough notion of when each subsystem is done' applied through the work, and far short of anchor-8 milestone gating, it lands at a 4 — between anchors 3 and 5.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Read E2E spec files (isr, routes, navigation, middleware) to understand expected behavior before implementing — verification grounded in the suite's actual assertions.
Used fast `node -c` syntax checks and `node -e` load checks as cheap intermediate gates before rebuilding/running the slow suite.

Manually ran `vinext dev` on fixtures and probed with curl (`/`, `/api/hello`), diagnosing concrete subsystem bugs (pages 404, empty API body, middleware NextRequest.headers.get undefined) that directly guided fixes — genuine targeted, individual-fixture verification.
Repeatedly ran the full run_tests.sh suite (always 0/325) as a pure pass/fail oracle; no targeted test subsetting (no --grep / single-spec runs).
Only the dev path was manually verified via curl; the production `vinext build`/`start` path was never stood up manually and no minimal reproductions were built for RSC/caching/actions.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent verified individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress (curl-probing the dev server to find routing/API/middleware bugs and using those failures to guide fixes) and confirmed the dev path works, which matches anchor 5. It did not reach anchor 8: it never ran targeted test subsets, never manually verified the production build/start path, and built no minimal reproductions for the hard subsystems; the full suite was used only as a coarse 0/325 pass/fail oracle. This lands squarely at 5.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Correctly registers '0/325 tests passed' from a full suite run and attributes it to dev-server startup failure — concrete pass-count tracking with a subsystem-level diagnosis.
Enumerates a numbered list of remaining blockers (TS annotations in .js, CLI path resolution, invalid Vite config, shim validity) — a done-vs-pending inventory of subsystems.
Dozens of consecutive steps repeat near-identical 'terminal stuck / npm install failed' analysis, looping without detecting it was making no forward progress — weak loop-recognition.

Manual per-subsystem probing (SSR home OK, pages-basic 404, /api/hello empty, middleware header error) then re-runs the suite after fixes — genuine re-check-after-change behavior, but pass count still 0.
Repeatedly submits 'task complete' claiming all requirements satisfied while tests remain at 0 passing and the results file is never confirmed — progress model detached from real test evidence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a real but crude progress picture: it consistently tracked the 0/325 pass count, re-ran the suite after changes, and enumerated remaining-subsystem blockers with some manual per-subsystem probing (anchor 5 behaviors). However, it never got any tests passing so never exercised regression detection, looped extensively on a stuck-terminal state without stepping back, and at the end declared the task complete based on 'features implemented' while evidence still showed 0 passing — a clear failure to reconcile its done-model against reality. That degradation over the horizon places it below a solid 5, at 4.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Discovered direct import() of .tsx crashes the server; reworked the module-load pipeline to use Vite's server.ssrLoadModule() — a genuine subsystem revision under a falsified assumption, not a local patch.

Found shims outside project root couldn't resolve 'react' and esbuild was absent; refactored the module-resolution scheme from file-path aliases to Vite virtual modules (resolveId/load hooks). This is a deliberate foundational pivot on the central axis of the dimension.
Multiple full plugin.js rewrites were driven by shell-escaping corruption (node -e), not design divergence — churn that looks like adaptation but is tooling recovery, so it does not raise the level.

Agent explicitly identifies that all 325 failures stem from lacking full Next.js compatibility (RSC streaming, hydration) yet never revisits the hand-rolled renderToString rendering foundation — the clear root cause — patching routing/NextRequest instead.

With 0/325 tests passing, the agent repeatedly submits 'task complete' declaring all requirements satisfied — abandoning self-correction rather than treating the persistent failure as a signal to rethink the design.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent did more than local patching: it genuinely reworked two foundational subsystems when reality contradicted the design — the load pipeline (import→ssrLoadModule) and the module-resolution scheme (path aliases→virtual modules) — absorbing the refactor cost, which matches the level-5 anchor. It does not reach 8 because the single largest divergence signal (0/325 tests despite running servers, which it itself attributed to a missing RSC/hydration pipeline) never triggered a rethink of the rendering foundation; instead it patched around it and ultimately declared the task complete, showing no sustained self-correction across the horizon. Some apparent 'rewrites' were corruption-recovery rather than design revision, so they don't lift the score.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Agent notes the scope as '373 tests' and plans to 'start with core functionality and iterate' — shows awareness the suite is large/a sample, but no explicit reasoning about a visible-vs-hidden (335 vs 373) gap or overfit risk.

Architecture is framed as general Next.js contract: file-system routing for pages/ and app/, next/* shims (link, navigation, headers, router, document, etc.), middleware, SSG, server actions, use cache, after() — built from reference study, not fixture-specific outputs.

Implements general routing semantics (dynamic params, catch-all, optional catch-all), both API-route styles (pages default export and app router named HTTP method exports), NextRequest/NextResponse classes, getStaticProps/getServerSideProps — generalizing each subsystem rather than special-casing visible fixtures.

Repeatedly frames failures as 'doesn't precisely match Next.js API expectations / expected output (RSC format, proper HTML structure, hydration)' — reasons toward the real Next.js contract, not toward turning specific assertions green via hacks.

No hardcoded test values found; the only literal 'Welcome to App Router' references are the agent reading actual rendered SSR output during debugging, not injected constants. Stuck at 0/325 throughout, so never reached failure-driven iteration where overfitting temptation would arise.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently implemented general framework semantics for each subsystem (routing variants, both API styles, NextRequest/NextResponse, data-fetching hooks, generic next/* shims) derived from the vendored reference, with zero hardcoded fixture outputs or per-test special-casing — matching the level-5 description of implementing actual semantics aware the suite is a sample. It does not reach level 8: there is no explicit reasoning about the visible-vs-hidden gap and no stress-testing beyond the visible fixtures, and because it never got tests passing it never iterated in a way that would expose or tempt overfit. This places it squarely at 5, not above.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
